answer.summary: Lowenhar’s warning is to hire for the work the startup needs next—not simply fill a senior job title. If the task is creating a playbook from scratch, seek an architect who has built one, rather than someone suited to optimizing an existing playbook.

sections.heading: Match the executive to the stage of work
sections.content: Lowenhar calls the person who builds a sales playbook from the founder’s methods an “architect.” They stay close to the founder, learn how deals are closed, and codify that process so the first account executives have structure. By contrast, an “optimizer” improves an existing playbook as the sales team grows. So the mistake is hiring for the wrong kind of executive experience—such as optimization experience when the company still needs someone to create the playbook.

sections.heading: Define the outcome before starting the search
sections.content: Lowenhar says to begin with what should have changed in the business 12 months after the hire, document what success looks like, and look for candidates who have already done that work. He warns against starting with a job description or treating a candidate’s experience at well-known companies as enough evidence by itself.

He advises defining what success should look like 12 months after the hire and looking for someone who has already done that work—not starting with a job description or simply gambling on a familiar company name.

answer.summary: Don’t hire for the wrong stage: when there’s no playbook yet, hire an architect who has already built one, rather than someone whose strength is optimizing or scaling an existing process.

sections.heading: The mistake to avoid
sections.content: Lowenhar distinguishes an “architect,” who builds the first playbook, from an “optimizer,” who improves an existing one, and a “scaler,” who grows the operation. So choosing someone suited to optimization or scaling when the job is to create the playbook is the mismatch to avoid. His broader hiring advice is to identify what success should look like and seek someone who has already done that work, rather than starting with a job description. Applying those points to this situation is a synthesis of his recommendations.

sections.heading: What the architect does
sections.content: In his sales example, the architect stays close to the founder, listens and observes—including reviewing recordings—and draws out how the founder closes deals. They codify that approach into the first playbook so the first account executives can follow a structure and succeed.
